_directions.plain: Plain and few: the reader’s present uncertainty, one short line per block, quiet org nudge.

plain.name: Dr San · Psychosocial Retirement Educator
plain.h1: Not sure what retirement will actually feel like?

built.name: Dr San · Psychosocial Retirement Educator
built.h1: Retiring soon, and not sure what comes next?
built.lede: Human-centred retirement planning, for your psychological and social wellbeing.

words.h: Most people plan the last Friday. Very few plan the Monday after.
words.sub: The calendar with nothing in it.
words.line: Only Monday is left. Nothing in it.

built.h: What catches people out is Monday.
built.sub: The calendar with nothing in it.
built.line: Only Monday is left. Nothing in it.

words.line: Your work quietly holds four things. All four leave on your last afternoon.

built.line: Four things are attached to your work, and all four leave on the same afternoon.

plain.lede: Four things leave with the job. Preparation puts them back.
plain.d1: Somewhere to be, every weekday. Then nowhere.
plain.d2: An easy answer to “what do you do?”
plain.d3: A reason to get going, handed to you each day.
plain.d4: Friends who were there because the work was.
plain.close: Each of these can be put back, with a plan.

words.lede: Four things leave on the same afternoon. Preparation is what puts them back.
words.d1: Forty years of somewhere to be. Then a Friday, and nowhere.
words.d2: Thirty years of an easy answer to “what do you do?”
words.d3: Work answered “what am I for?” every day. The question doesn’t retire.
words.d4: Most work friends were there because the work was.
words.close: Every one of these can be put back. That is the part of the plan I help with.

built.lede: Four things leave on the same afternoon. Preparation is what puts them back.
built.d1: Forty years of somewhere to be. Then a Friday, and nowhere.
built.d2: Thirty years of an easy answer to “what do you do?”
built.d3: Work answered “what am I for?” every day. The question doesn’t retire.
built.d4: Most work friends were there because the work was.
built.close: Every one of these can be put back. It takes a plan, the same as the money did.

words.ask: So why does nobody make one?
words.lede: Most of us spend forty years planning retirement financially, and roughly ten minutes on who we’ll be when it arrives.
words.close: Money funds a lifestyle. It has never once told anyone what to do with a Wednesday.

built.ask: So why does nobody make one?
built.lede: We spend forty years planning for retirement financially and roughly ten minutes planning who we will be when it arrives.
built.close: Money funds a lifestyle. It has never once told anyone what to do with a Wednesday.

words.h: I work with people, and with the organisations they work for.
words.p1: Three to ten years out is the easiest time to start. You still have time, colleagues and energy.
words.p2: I run workshops, seminars and training for staff getting close to retirement.

built.h: I work with people, and with the organisations they work for.
built.p1: You still have time, colleagues, energy and a title that opens doors. That is the cheap end — the work gets more expensive the longer you wait.
built.p2: Australians are retiring faster than at any point in the nation's history, and thirty years of institutional knowledge can leave in a single quarter.

plain.role: Psychosocial retirement educator  ·  Far North Queensland
plain.lede1: Known as Dr San. She works with people three to ten years from retirement, and with the organisations they work for.
plain.lede2: She isn’t a financial adviser. She helps with the rest of the plan: your days, your sense of self, your people.

built.role: Psychosocial retirement educator  ·  Far North Queensland
built.lede1:
Known as Dr San. She works with individuals who are three to ten years from a
        retirement date, and with the HR and workforce planners who are about to lose thirty
        years of institutional knowledge in a single quarter.
built.lede2:
She is not a financial adviser and has no interest in becoming one. She teaches the
        other half of the plan — the half that decides whether the first half was worth
        doing.

plain.m1: Hi, lovely to hear from you. What date are we working towards?
plain.m2: Retiring in March! Super's all sorted, the adviser's been great.
plain.m3: Wonderful news. And what does an ordinary Tuesday look like after that?
plain.m4: Ha — hadn't thought that far. Probably just... home, I suppose.
plain.m5: No rush to have it figured out. That's exactly what we'd chat about.
plain.m6: Thirty minutes, no cost — just a chat. Would you like to find a time?
plain.h: A free 30-minute chat, well before the date.
plain.lede: About what your weeks might look like. Not an assessment.

plain.h: A money plan covers the money.
plain.lede: The lower half isn’t a money problem, so it was never going to reach it.
plain.comment: One pays for the life. The other helps you live it.

words.h: Your money plan is doing its job.
words.lede: The lower half is the part it was never built for. It’s the part I help with.
words.comment: One funds the lifestyle. The other decides whether there is a life in it.

built.h: A money plan is excellent at the things it covers.
